title: ParticleDB fails ACID promises and other Sunday dev stories
excerpt: Jepsen found 96 issues in ParticleDB, a Lenovo USB stick held an unencrypted SD card, Karpathy built HackerTube in two hours, and a Linux TCP bug needs a kernel update.
body:
ParticleDB’s landing page boasted “Full ACID” and 159 K transactions per second. Lenovo marketed the ThinkPlus FU100 stick as an AES-256 hardware-encrypted USB key. Andrej Karpathy posted a video showing a site called HackerTube that scraped 6 454 Hacker News-recommended videos in a single afternoon. The same roundup also warned about a critical IPv4 TCP use-after-free in the Linux kernel (CVE-2026-98432) with a CVSS score of 9.8.  

In the next few paragraphs you will see what Jepsen uncovered in ParticleDB, what a researcher discovered inside Lenovo’s “encrypted” stick, how Karpathy turned a comment dump into a functional video catalog in two hours, and the exact steps needed to protect a Linux host from the TCP bug. The goal is to leave you with concrete actions: verify isolation guarantees before deploying a database, confirm hardware-encryption claims with independent testing, and apply the kernel patch for CVE-2026-98432 without delay.

## Jepsen finds 96 safety issues in ParticleDB  

Jepsen, the database-testing lab run by Kyle Kingsbury, published its analysis of ParticleDB 1.1.4 on 31 October 2026. The Rust-based store, built by Orkes for AI workloads, advertises a Postgres-compatible interface, key-value access, vector search, and user-defined functions. The test covered every public build from 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.11.rc-22 and logged 96 distinct problems.  

The homepage claim “Full ACID. 159 K TPS.” conflicted with the actual isolation level. The banner described snapshot isolation, which does not guarantee serializable behavior, and the isolation mode was controlled by a startup flag (`--txn-mode`) rather than the standard SQL `SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL` statements. Jepsen noted that no TLA⁺ specification, despite the “formally proven” badge, was supplied during the collaboration.  

Most failures required only a single server and a single client, with no injected network faults. For example, a query `WHERE 4 = 5` returned a row with primary key 5, an `UPDATE` could leave two rows sharing the same primary key, aborted transactions sometimes appeared committed, and rows from a dropped table re-emerged in mangled form.

By version 1.1.18.11.rc-22, all but ten issues were resolved; two serious problems persisted: the default OCC mode regularly lost committed writes, and the strictest serializable mode still produced lost updates when Jepsen killed the process.

Orkes released 1.1.19-rc.13 claiming all remaining issues were fixed, but Jepsen has not yet evaluated that build. The report concludes with a clear recommendation: halt further deployment of ParticleDB and migrate to a database with proven isolation guarantees. The full analysis is available in the [Jepsen report on dev.to](https://dev.to/axrisi/particledbs-jepsen-report-lenovos-fingerprint-usb-stick-karpathys-hackertube-and-the-linux-tcp-4nbc).

## Lenovo’s “hardware-encrypted” USB stick contains a plain SD card  

Researcher Xusheng Li purchased a Lenovo ThinkPlus FU100 fingerprint USB stick that was marketed as an AES-256 hardware-encrypted storage device. After opening the metal enclosure, Li discovered a standard micro-SD card with no encryption layer applied to the flash memory. The firmware presented a “hardware encrypted” label, yet the storage medium was ordinary and empty.  

The finding undermines the product’s security claims and demonstrates why independent hardware audits are essential. A device that advertises AES-256 encryption should either perform encryption on-chip or expose a verifiable cryptographic module; a plain SD card offers no such guarantee. The dev.to article that aggregates the four stories provides the full details of Li’s teardown.

## Karpathy builds HackerTube in two hours  

Andrej Karpathy set out to create a searchable video archive of every link that had been recommended in Hacker News comment threads. The result, HackerTube, lists 6 454 videos and was assembled in roughly two hours.

The workflow consisted of pulling the latest Hacker News comment dump (a JSON file of several hundred megabytes), running a short Python script that extracts YouTube URLs, de-duplicates them, and writes a simple Markdown index, then feeding the Markdown file to a static-site generator such as Hugo.

A snippet of the extraction script illustrates the simplicity:

```python
import json, re, pathlib

data = json.loads(pathlib.Path('hn_comments.json').read_text())
yt_links = {m.group(0) for c in data for m in re.finditer(r'https?://youtu\.be/\\w+', c['text'])}
with open('content/_index.md', 'w') as f:
    for url in sorted(yt_links):
        f.write(f'* [{url}]({url})\\n')
```

The rapid turnaround shows that when source data is already well-structured, a few lines of code can turn a massive comment thread into a functional website. The dev.to post includes a link to the full walkthrough.

## Patch the Linux TCP use-after-free bug (CVE-2026-98432)  

CVE-2026-98432 is an IPv4 TCP use-after-free vulnerability in the Linux kernel. The bug occurs when the kernel frees a TCP socket structure while a lingering reference still exists, allowing an attacker to trigger arbitrary code execution. All major distributions have back-ported the fix to their stable kernel branches.  

To remediate the issue, follow these steps:

1. Identify the fixed kernel version for your distribution.  
2. Update the kernel package (`sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install linux-image-generic` on Debian/Ubuntu, `sudo dnf update kernel` on Fedora, `sudo pacman -Syu linux` on Arch).  
3. Reboot to load the patched kernel (`sudo reboot`).  
4. Verify the running kernel includes the fix (`uname -r` should show the version installed in step 2).

If the kernel version is older than the patched release, the system remains vulnerable. The dev.to roundup notes that the patch is already present in current releases, but administrators must still confirm they are running the updated image.

## The takeaway  

ParticleDB’s “Full ACID” banner does not survive rigorous testing; treat isolation claims skeptically and run your own consistency checks before production rollout. Lenovo’s fingerprint stick proves that hardware-encryption labels can be misleading, so verify the actual storage medium when security matters. Karpathy’s two-hour build demonstrates that a well-structured data dump can be turned into a usable site with a few lines of script. Finally, protect any Linux host from CVE-2026-98432 by installing the distribution’s fixed kernel and rebooting.
